title: 10,500-year-old timbers emerge from german lakebed
dek: Worked wood and stone tools found 20 metres under lake water.
body: About 20 metres below the surface of Lake Arendsee in Saxony-Anhalt, underwater archaeologists have recovered 10,500-year-old worked timbers, stone tools and animal bones. The finds come from a submerged prehistoric landscape that researchers have been investigating since spring 2026. A wooden post, 1.6 metres long, preserves clear evidence of felling and working, while split planks up to 1.3 metres long were also recovered.

Researchers from the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology of Saxony-Anhalt made the discovery. Among the most significant pieces is timber that may have formed part of a constructed feature, possibly even a hut. However, no building plan or other evidence has yet established that the wood formed part of a dwelling. Describing the site as a permanent settlement remains premature; the finds demonstrate that Mesolithic people were active at the former lakeshore and were working substantial pieces of timber there.

Around 10,500 years ago, communities in Central Europe relied on hunting, fishing and gathering rather than agriculture. Even if a structure is eventually identified at Arendsee, this would not necessarily indicate permanent occupation. Hunter-gatherer communities could construct substantial features at camps or other locations that were occupied temporarily or revisited seasonally. The importance of the discovery instead lies in the exceptional survival of worked wood from the Mesolithic period.

Evidence for structures from this period is often preserved only indirectly, through features such as postholes and changes in soil colour. The waterlogged environment at Arendsee has preserved the timber itself, including traces of prehistoric woodworking. A salt dome beneath the lake has caused sections of the lakebed to gradually submerge, covering archaeological remains along ancient shores and creating conditions capable of preserving organic material such as wood.

The lake has already produced discoveries from several periods, including Neolithic fish weirs and medieval watercraft. Researchers are now using underwater technology to investigate the prehistoric landscape in greater detail. A remotely operated underwater vehicle, deployed in collaboration with researchers from the Fraunhofer Institute in Ilmenau, has produced high-resolution sonar imagery of the former shoreline. The survey is helping archaeologists identify areas for future investigation and plan more targeted dives.

Researchers hope to conduct dendrochronological analysis using the surviving tree rings, although dating such ancient wood is challenging because suitable comparative material is scarce. The timbers are also expected to undergo magnetic resonance imaging in Halle to reveal additional information about their internal structure. Further dives will attempt to establish the extent of the archaeological remains and determine whether the individual pieces of worked wood were connected.

For now, the evidence supports the presence of Mesolithic people at the ancient lakeshore, but not yet the existence of a permanent settlement. Determining whether the timbers belonged to a hut, another type of structure or separate activities will be one of the central questions of future research at Lake Arendsee.
doesnt_show: The finds do not yet show whether the timbers formed part of a permanent dwelling or how long any occupation lasted.
settle: Targeted dives and dendrochronological analysis of the surviving wood would clarify the structure's function and duration of use.
